M02-RC-P01.x:
[¶1] On a moonless Friday, twelve students met beside a meadow carrying white sheets, flashlights, and notebooks. Their goal was to count moths for a community wildlife survey. Each team hung a sheet between two poles and shone a light toward it. Soon, tiny wings flickered out of the darkness. The students photographed each visitor, recorded the time, and let it fly away.

[¶2] At first, Lena's team thought its station was the most successful. Thirty-seven moths landed on its sheet, while a station near the pond attracted only nineteen. Then Lena noticed a problem: her team's lamp was brighter. A brighter lamp might draw moths from a wider area, making the stations impossible to compare fairly.

[¶3] The students did not throw away the evening's work. Instead, they added lamp brightness to their notes and repeated the count the following week using identical lights. This time, the pond station attracted the most moths. Several species there had narrow wings and muted colors that made them difficult to see until they settled on the sheet.

[¶4] The survey did more than produce a list. It showed the students why a fair comparison requires controlling important conditions. Their first count raised a useful question; their second count gave them stronger evidence. In science, an imperfect result can still be valuable when it helps improve the next investigation.

M02-RC-P02.x:
[¶1] When workers removed the worn front steps of Bellweather's town hall, they uncovered a flat stone carved with a triangle and the date 1882. Most residents assumed it was a decoration. Town archivist Imani Cho suspected otherwise because the triangle matched a symbol drawn on early survey maps.

[¶2] In the nineteenth century, surveyors often placed durable markers at carefully measured locations. Later mapmakers could begin from those fixed points instead of measuring an entire region again. Imani found a field notebook explaining that Bellweather's marker once stood in open ground. The town hall had been built around it decades later, and the front steps had hidden it.

[¶3] The discovery created a practical puzzle. The builders needed to pour a new foundation, but moving the marker would erase its value as a record of the original location. Imani, the engineer, and the construction crew designed a solution: they left the stone undisturbed and built a small glass panel into the new landing. Visitors could see the marker without stepping on it.

[¶4] The stone did not reveal buried treasure or a forgotten tunnel. Its importance was quieter. It connected modern measurements to the work of people who had mapped the town more than a century earlier. By building around it once again—this time deliberately—the town preserved both a useful reference point and a piece of its own story.

M02-RC-P03.x:
[¶1] Mara had chosen the window seat before the train left the station, but she spent the first hour looking at everything except the view. She counted the stitches in her backpack strap, reorganized three pencils, and checked the envelope in her pocket twice. Inside it was the story she planned to read at the youth festival. “Planned” was perhaps too confident a word.

[¶2] Across the aisle, an older man was sketching passengers. His pencil moved quickly, pausing only when the train rocked. When he noticed Mara watching, he turned the page toward her. The drawing showed a child asleep under a coat, a conductor leaning around a seat, and Mara gripping her envelope as if it might escape.

[¶3] “You made everyone look calm,” Mara said.

“They weren't holding still,” the man replied. “I just chose which moments to keep.” He tapped Mara's drawn hand. “That one looked determined.”

[¶4] Mara almost explained that determined people did not consider missing their stop on purpose. Instead, she looked out the window. Telephone poles appeared and vanished. Farmhouses flashed between rows of trees. No single view lasted long, yet the trip held together. She opened the envelope and read her first paragraph under her breath. By the time the train slowed at the festival town, the paper no longer shook.

M02-RC-P04.x:
[¶1] Choreographer Suri Patel had eight dancers but no rehearsal room large enough for the new piece. The community hall was available only on Saturdays, and its polished floor could not be marked with tape. Suri needed a way to test complicated pathways before the dancers arrived.

[¶2] She went to an empty basketball court with a box of sidewalk chalk. On the pavement, she drew circles for starting positions and arrows for movement. Blue arrows curved toward the center; yellow ones crossed them; white dotted lines showed moments when dancers moved backward. From the bleachers, the design looked like a map of several windy roads.

[¶3] The chalk plan revealed a collision before anyone took a step. Two arrows met at the same place on the same count. Suri shifted one pathway, then walked every route herself while counting the music. Rain erased the drawing that night, but by then Suri had photographed each section and copied the changes into her notebook.

[¶4] At Saturday's rehearsal, the dancers learned the opening without colliding. The chalk drawing had not replaced rehearsal: it could not show whether a lift felt safe or a turn matched the music. It had done something else. By making invisible movement visible, it let Suri solve one kind of problem early and save precious hall time for the problems only dancers could answer.

M02-RC-P05.x:
[¶1] The new bus shelter outside Juniper Middle School looked ordinary except for its roof, which was covered with shallow trays of tough, low-growing plants. During the first heavy rain, students noticed water dripping from the roof long after the storm had passed. Some assumed the shelter was leaking.

[¶2] It was actually working as designed. Soil and plant roots held part of the rainfall, while small channels released extra water slowly into a barrel. A bare metal roof would have sent most water rushing toward the sidewalk at once. The planted roof delayed that flow, reducing puddles near the curb.

[¶3] The environmental club measured water in the barrel after three storms. The largest storm did not produce the fullest barrel. It came after several dry, windy days, so the soil absorbed much of the rain. A smaller storm that arrived when the soil was already damp sent more water through the channels. The students realized that storm size was not the only factor affecting runoff.

[¶4] In spring, the club will compare temperatures beneath the planted shelter and an unplanted shelter across the street. They predict that shade from leaves and moisture in the soil may keep the planted roof cooler. Whether or not the prediction is correct, the students now know to record starting conditions, not merely the final measurement.

all.e: C combines the roof's function [¶2] with the students' learning [¶3–¶4]. A and D are unsupported—the club measured rather than rebuilt—and B mistakes delayed release for a leak.
all.q: Which choice best connects the roof's function with the students' investigation?

c: Dry soil absorbed much of its rain.
Students emptied the barrel during the storm.
The plants blocked every drainage channel.
Strong wind blew the barrel onto its side.

all.q: Why did the largest storm not fill the barrel the most?

To find out whether a bare metal roof can collect any rain
To prove that the planted shelter never becomes warm in spring
To isolate whether the planted roof is related to temperature

water that flows off a surface
a test that ends too early

all.q: In [¶3], “runoff” most nearly means:

c: To show that recording conditions can guide a new investigation
To prove that the school's rain barrel was installed incorrectly
To introduce a disagreement between two student science clubs
To explain why spring storms are heavier than winter storms

all.e: 4,608 + 2,795 = 7,403; B and D reflect carrying errors, and C drops one thousand.
all.q: A reading drive collected 4,608 books in spring and 2,795 in fall. How many books were collected altogether?

all.e: With denominator 24, 21/24 − 8/24 = 13/24. A subtracts denominators, B changes only the numerator, and D uses an incorrect common denominator.

all.e: 4.75 × 6 = 28.50. A multiplies only the dollars (4 × 6 = 24) and appends the 75 cents, C swaps the cents digits of 28.50, and D rounds to $5 × 6 = $30 and then adds the 75 cents back.
all.q: Six identical notebooks cost $4.75 each. What is the total cost?

all.e: 945 ÷ 15 = 63 because 15 × 63 = 945; the other choices come from incomplete division or rounding.
all.q: A printer places 945 cards equally into 15 boxes. How many cards are in each box?

all.e: 0.35 × 240 = 84; A finds 30%, B finds one third approximately, and D finds 40%.
all.q: A 240-page book has illustrations on 35% of its pages. How many pages have illustrations?

all.e: Common factors include 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 18; 18 is greatest. B and C are common but not greatest, while D is a multiple.
all.q: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 54?

all.e: 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12, and whole parts total 5. The distractors add denominators or regroup incorrectly.

all.e: Subtract 7 from both sides to get 5x = 35, then divide by 5 for x = 7. A divides 35 by the constant 7 instead of by 5, C follows a subtraction slip (42 − 7 taken as 45, giving 45 ÷ 5 = 9), and D adds 7 to 42 before dividing (49 ÷ 5).
all.q: Solve 5x + 7 = 42.

all.e: 4² = 16, then 3 × 16 − 5 = 43. A squares after multiplying incorrectly, and B or C reflect arithmetic errors.
all.q: What is the value of 3x² − 5 when x = 4?

all.e: Multiply both terms by 6: 6y + 18. B fails to distribute to 3, while C and D combine unlike terms.
all.q: Which expression is equivalent to 6(y + 3)?

all.e: Multiplying both sides by positive 4 gives n < 24; B reverses the sign, and A or D use wrong operations.
all.q: Which inequality is equivalent to n/4 < 6?

all.e: Triangle angles total 180°; 180 − (48 + 67) = 65°. The distractors reflect addition or subtraction errors.
all.q: Two angles of a triangle measure 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?

all.e: Area = base × perpendicular height = 13 × 8 = 104 cm². A uses perimeter-like addition, C multiplies incorrectly, and D doubles the area.
all.q: A parallelogram has a base of 13 cm and a perpendicular height of 8 cm. What is its area?

all.e: Radius is half the diameter, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 feet. A doubles, B repeats the diameter, and D divides by three.
all.q: A circular table has a diameter of 18 feet. What is its radius?

all.e: Volume = 7 × 4 × 3 = 84 cubic feet. B multiplies only length and width (7 × 4 = 28), while C and D first add all three dimensions (7 + 4 + 3 = 14) and then multiply by the height (14 × 3 = 42) or the length (14 × 7 = 98) instead of multiplying all three dimensions.
all.q: A storage box is 7 feet long, 4 feet wide, and 3 feet high. What is its volume?

all.e: One meter is 100 centimeters, so 2.35 × 100 = 235 cm. A multiplies by 10, B makes no unit-size adjustment, and D multiplies by 10,000.
all.q: A ribbon is 2.35 meters long. How many centimeters long is it?

all.e: 3:40 + 2 hours = 5:40, plus 35 minutes = 6:15. The distractors omit time or fail to regroup 60 minutes.

all.e: The sum is 85, and 85 ÷ 5 = 17. The other choices result from choosing a middle or dividing incorrectly.
all.q: What is the mean of 12, 15, 17, 20, and 21?
